title: Sky and space
subtitle: Moons, stars and space firsts
about: Moons of the Solar System, the brightest stars and the landmarks of the southern sky as seen from New Zealand, and the firsts of the space age. Where a first is contested, the card names exactly what was achieved.

cards.prompt: Largest moon relative to the size of its planet
cards.note: Its diameter is roughly a quarter of Earth's; it is also the fifth-largest moon in the Solar System.

cards.prompt: Largest moon in the Solar System
cards.note: Larger than Mercury but under half its mass, it is the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field.
The only moon with a dense atmosphere, mostly nitrogen; the surface pressure is about 1.45 times Earth's at sea level.
Found by William Herschel in 1787 and named after the fairy queen in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers rising up to 8 km in 1989; its surface, near 38 K, is among the coldest known.
Half Pluto's diameter, it puts their barycentre outside Pluto; the pair are mutually tidally locked, each always showing the same face.
It orbits faster than Mars rotates, so it rises in the west; tides shrink its orbit by about 2 m per century.
Named after Dread, who joins Fear in the Iliad; tidal acceleration is slowly enlarging its orbit, unlike that of Phobos.

cards.prompt: Most volcanically active body in the Solar System
cards.note: Tidal flexing, sustained by its 1:2:4 orbital resonance with Europa and Ganymede, powers more than 400 active volcanoes.

cards.prompt: Smallest Galilean moon, with an ocean beneath its ice
cards.note: The smoothest known object in the Solar System; its hidden ocean may hold two to three times the water in Earth's oceans.

cards.prompt: Galilean moon with the oldest, most cratered surface
cards.note: Outside the orbital resonance of the inner three, it suffers little tidal heating; its Valhalla impact basin is ringed by vast concentric ridges.

cards.prompt: Moon with seas of liquid methane and ethane
cards.note: Apart from Earth, the only known body with stable liquid on its surface; Kraken Mare, near the north pole, is the largest sea.

cards.prompt: Saturn moon whose south-pole geysers feed the E ring
cards.note: Fresh snow makes it one of the most reflective bodies in the Solar System; the jets tap a global ocean beneath the ice.

cards.prompt: Saturn moon whose giant crater recalls the Death Star
cards.note: Herschel crater spans about a third of its diameter; resonance with Mimas clears the Cassini Division in Saturn's rings.

cards.prompt: Saturn moon with one dark and one bright hemisphere
cards.note: Cassini found it in 1671 but could see it on only one side of Saturn, and rightly deduced a dark hemisphere.

cards.prompt: Sponge-like Saturn moon with a chaotic rotation
cards.note: The first non-round moon discovered, in 1848; its porous body tumbles unpredictably, influenced by a 3:4 resonance with Titan.
Found by Pickering in 1899; its retrograde orbit suggests a captured centaur, and its dust forms the vast Phoebe ring.
Roughly three-quarters ice; a 2008 suggestion that it had rings of its own was not confirmed by later Cassini observations.

cards.prompt: Saturn moons that swap orbits every four years
cards.note: Their mean orbits differ by only 50 km; this horseshoe exchange is the only known configuration of its kind among moons.

cards.prompt: Walnut-shaped moon that clears Saturn's Encke Gap
cards.note: Its equatorial ridge is ring material it has swept up; Mark Showalter found it in 1990 in old Voyager 2 images.

cards.prompt: Uranus moon with perhaps the tallest cliff in the Solar System
cards.note: Verona Rupes is about 20 km high; the patchwork surface may record tidal heating during a past resonance with Umbriel.

cards.prompt: Outermost of the five major moons of Uranus
cards.note: Found by Herschel the same night as Titania in 1787, and named after the fairy king in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Named after the spirit in The Tempest and a sylph in Pope's poem; some of its plains may be under 100 million years old.

cards.prompt: Darkest of the major moons of Uranus
cards.note: Named after a melancholy sprite in Pope's The Rape of the Lock, from the Latin umbra; a bright ring marks Wunda crater.

cards.prompt: Only large moon with a retrograde orbit
cards.note: Orbiting against its planet's spin points to capture: Triton was probably once a dwarf planet from the Kuiper belt.

cards.prompt: Neptune moon with a highly eccentric, year-long orbit
cards.note: With eccentricity 0.75, its distance from Neptune swings between about 1.4 and 9.7 million km; Kuiper discovered it in 1949.

cards.prompt: First moon of an asteroid to be discovered
cards.note: The Galileo spacecraft imaged it in 1993 while passing asteroid 243 Ida; it is only about 1.6 km long.

cards.prompt: Asteroid moonlet struck by NASA's DART probe
cards.note: The 2022 impact cut its 11 hour 55 minute orbit of Didymos by about 33 minutes, the first test of asteroid deflection.
The brightest star in the night sky, at magnitude −1.46, partly because it is only 8.6 light-years away; Māori call it Takurua.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Second-brightest star in the night sky; Māori call it Atutahi, and spacecraft star trackers have used it to fix their orientation.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: A pair 4.34 light-years away: Rigil Kentaurus and Toliman orbit each other every 80 years, with Proxima a distant third.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: A red dwarf 4.25 light-years away, too faint to see with the naked eye; it hosts at least two confirmed planets.
Māori call it Māhutonga; extending the line from Gacrux through Acrux about 4.5 times locates the south celestial pole.
The foot of the Southern Cross, about 350 light-years away; the single point we see is a multiple system of hot B-type stars.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: A hot blue giant about 280 light-years away, only 8 to 11 million years old and massive enough to end as a supernova.
cards.label: Second-brightest star in

cards.prompt: Red giant at the top of the Southern Cross
cards.note: About 89 light-years away, it is the nearest M-type red giant to the Sun; its orange-red tint shows to the naked eye.

cards.prompt: Inner pointer to the Southern Cross
cards.note: Beta Centauri is a triple system about 360 light-years away, more than 80 times farther than the outer pointer, Alpha Centauri.

cards.prompt: Dark nebula beside the Southern Cross
cards.note: A dust cloud about 590 light-years away that blocks background starlight; in Aboriginal astronomy it is the head of the Emu in the Sky.

cards.prompt: Star cluster called Matariki in te reo Māori
cards.note: Its dawn rising in midwinter signals the Māori New Year, an official public holiday in New Zealand since 2022.
About 163,000 light-years away; neutrinos from the supernova arrived hours before its light, the first ever detected from a supernova.

cards.prompt: Dwarf galaxy in Tucana visible to the naked eye
cards.note: Henrietta Leavitt's study of its Cepheid variables revealed the period-luminosity relation, a key rung of the cosmic distance ladder.

cards.prompt: Largest globular cluster in the Milky Way
cards.note: About 10 million stars, 17,000 light-years away; it may be the core of a dwarf galaxy disrupted and absorbed by the Milky Way.
Its Great Dimming of 2019 to 2020, a roughly threefold fall in brightness, was caused by dust from a surface mass ejection.
A blue supergiant about 850 light-years away; as Puanga, its dawn rising marks the Māori New Year for some iwi.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Within 0.7 degrees of the north celestial pole, so it never rises from New Zealand; it is also the nearest Cepheid variable.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.prompt: Faint star nearest the south celestial pole
cards.note: At magnitude 5.5 and about one degree from the pole, it is the dimmest star shown on any national flag, Brazil's.
The brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere, an orange giant 37 light-years away whose light opened Chicago's 1933 World's Fair.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Long the zero point of the magnitude scale; in 1850 it became the first star other than the Sun to be photographed.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Not one star but four, in two binary pairs: a close pair of yellow giants and a fainter, distant pair, 43 light-years away.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Its Greek name means 'before the dog' because it rises ahead of Sirius; like Sirius, it has a white dwarf companion.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: It spins so fast that its equatorial diameter is about 35% larger than its polar one; the name means 'end of the river'.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: It spins in under eight hours, flattening it; it was the first main-sequence star other than the Sun to have its surface imaged.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Arabic for 'the follower', as it trails the Pleiades; it lies well in front of the Hyades cluster, 67 against 150 light-years.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: A red supergiant named 'rival to Ares' for its Mars-like colour; Māori call it Rēhua and regard it as chief of all stars.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Its Arabic name means 'the raised tail', as it marks the scorpion's sting; it is a triple system about 570 light-years away.
cards.label: Second-brightest star in

cards.note: Its two main stars orbit every four days, distorting each other into ellipsoids; Hipparchus's data on it led him to precession.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Though designated beta, it outshines alpha Castor; at 34 light-years it is the nearest giant star, and has a planet named Thestias.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.prompt: Gemini star that is really six stars
cards.note: Three visual components, each a spectroscopic binary; the two brightest pairs orbit each other every 459 years, 49 light-years away.
Ringed by debris discs; its once-celebrated planet, Fomalhaut b, now appears to be an expanding cloud of debris from a collision.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: A blue supergiant 1,400 to 2,600 light-years away, among the most luminous first-magnitude stars; its name is Arabic for 'tail'.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: Only 0.47 degrees from the ecliptic, it is often occulted by the Moon; it spins every 15.9 hours, close to breakup speed.
cards.label: Brightest star in

cards.note: About 4.7 million years ago it was the brightest star in our sky, at magnitude −3.99; it is now the sky's brightest extreme-ultraviolet source.
cards.label: Second-brightest star in

cards.note: Latin for 'wonderful'; it brightens and fades over about 332 days, and GALEX found it trailing a tail 13 light-years long.

cards.prompt: Eclipsing binary known as the Demon Star
cards.note: It dims from magnitude 2.1 to 3.4 every 2.86 days; John Goodricke proposed in 1783 that a dark body passes in front.
It covers 1,303 square degrees; its brightest star, Alphard, means 'the solitary one', having few bright neighbours.

cards.label: First
cards.note: A 58 cm, 83.6 kg sphere orbiting every 96 minutes; drag on its orbit revealed the density of the upper atmosphere.

cards.label: First
cards.note: She flew on Sputnik 2; officials hid for decades that she died of overheating within hours, which was revealed only in 2002.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to detect the Van Allen belts
cards.note: Its Geiger counter read zero at high altitude, saturated by trapped particles; James Van Allen's team realised why.

cards.label: First
cards.note: It struck east of Mare Imbrium in September 1959, the first human-made object to reach another celestial body.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to photograph the Moon's far side
cards.note: It developed its film on board, then scanned it for radio transmission, imaging about 70% of the far side.

cards.label: First
cards.note: Vostok 1 made one orbit in about 108 minutes; Gagarin ejected at 7 km and landed separately by parachute.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to fly successfully past another planet
cards.note: Passing Venus, it measured a very hot surface, and on the way confirmed that the solar wind streams continuously.

cards.label: First
cards.note: She flew Vostok 6 alone for nearly three days and 48 orbits, and remains the only woman to have flown a solo mission.

cards.label: First
cards.note: Outside Voskhod 2 for about 12 minutes, his suit ballooned in the vacuum, so he bled off pressure to squeeze back in.

cards.label: First
cards.note: Its images showed a cratered surface; radio occultation revealed a surface pressure under 1% of Earth's.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to soft-land on the Moon
cards.note: Its photos showed the ground could bear a lander; Jodrell Bank decoded the signal, and a British newspaper published them first.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Crewed spacecraft to orbit the Moon
cards.note: Borman, Lovell and Anders made ten lunar orbits, becoming the first humans to see the far side with their own eyes.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: People to walk on the Moon
cards.note: They landed Eagle in the Sea of Tranquility while Michael Collins orbited in Columbia, and collected 21.5 kg of samples.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to transmit from another planet's surface
cards.note: Faint signals found on tape revealed about 475 °C and roughly 90 times Earth's sea-level pressure on Venus.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Robotic rover to drive on another world
cards.note: Driven from Earth, it covered 10.5 km; found again in 2010, its French laser retroreflector was then used for laser ranging.

cards.label: First
cards.note: Its only crew, from Soyuz 11, died when their capsule lost its air during re-entry; they remain the only humans to die in space.

cards.label: First
cards.note: It arrived during a planet-wide dust storm, waited, then mapped 85% of Mars; Valles Marineris is named after it.

cards.label: First
cards.note: Transmission stopped about 20 seconds after it began, during a great dust storm, leaving only a grey image without detail.

cards.label: First
cards.note: It was also the first to cross the asteroid belt, and carries a plaque for any finder; its last signal came in 2003.

cards.label: First
cards.note: It was the first to use one planet's gravity, that of Venus, to reach another, and found Mercury's magnetic field.

cards.label: First
cards.note: It worked on the surface for over six years until 1982, a record not broken until the Opportunity rover in 2010.

cards.label: First
cards.note: It remains the only spacecraft to visit Uranus or Neptune, using a rare alignment of the outer planets in the late 1970s.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Space telescope designed to be serviced by astronauts
cards.note: Its 2.4 m mirror was ground about 2.2 micrometres too flat at the edge; corrective optics fitted in orbit in 1993 fixed it.

cards.label: First
cards.note: A 10.6 kg rover from Mars Pathfinder, named after abolitionist Sojourner Truth; it lasted 83 sols instead of the planned 8.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to land on an asteroid
cards.note: Built as an orbiter, it was eased down onto 433 Eros and survived, then measured surface composition with its gamma-ray spectrometer.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to land in the outer Solar System
cards.note: ESA's probe parachuted onto Titan, the farthest landing ever made, and found rounded water-ice pebbles on a dry lakebed.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to return asteroid samples to Earth
cards.note: Despite failing reaction wheels and ion engines, it brought back about 1,500 grains from Itokawa; its name means peregrine falcon.

cards.label: First
cards.note: It crossed the heliopause at about 121 AU, confirmed by a sharp jump in plasma density inferred from plasma oscillations.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to soft-land on a comet
cards.note: Its harpoons failed, so it bounced twice on comet 67P and settled in shadow, working on battery power for about 64 hours.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Orbital rocket to land its first stage vertically
cards.note: The booster touched down at Cape Canaveral after launching 11 Orbcomm satellites, and now stands outside SpaceX headquarters.

cards.label: First
cards.note: Launched at about 16.26 km/s relative to Earth, the fastest launch ever, it carries some of Clyde Tombaugh's ashes.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Rocket to reach orbit from New Zealand
cards.note: Launched from Māhia Peninsula; its Rutherford engines were the first electric-pump-fed engines to power an orbital-class rocket.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to land on the Moon's far side
cards.note: It landed in Von Kármán crater, talking to Earth through the Queqiao relay satellite near the Earth-Moon L2 point.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Telescope to image a black hole's shadow
cards.note: Linking radio dishes across Earth at 1.3 mm wavelength, it imaged M87*, a black hole of about 6.5 billion solar masses.

cards.label: Largest
cards.note: Its 6.5 m mirror of 18 gold-coated beryllium segments must stay below 50 K, shaded by a five-layer sunshield near Sun-Earth L2.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Aircraft to make a powered flight on another planet
cards.note: In Martian air about 1% as dense as Earth's, its rotors spun at over 2,400 rpm; it made 72 flights.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to fly through the Sun's corona
cards.note: It crossed the Alfvén critical surface in April 2021; it honours Eugene Parker, who predicted the solar wind in 1958.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Spacecraft to soft-land near the Moon's south pole
cards.note: Its Vikram lander set down near 69° S, making India the fourth nation to soft-land on the Moon.

cards.label: First
cards.prompt: Mission to return samples from the Moon's far side
cards.note: It brought back about 1,935 g from the Apollo basin, inside the vast South Pole-Aitken basin, possibly including mantle fragments.
